imageAlt: Illustrative skincare pump and refill pouch book box concept
title: Pump Bottle and Refill Pouch Gift Box: Fit Before Artwork
seoTitle: Pump Bottle and Refill Pouch Gift Box: Fit Before Artwork | MTT
summary: Plan a book-style gift box around the filled pouch, capped pump, insert and information card.
intro: The bottle may be rigid, but a filled refill pouch changes shape when laid flat. Before artwork is locked, agree its filled state, the orientation of its spout and the surface that supports it. Check the complete loaded sample with the actual pump, card and intended outer shipping pack.
cta: Send the actual product dimensions, quantity per design, destination and project details. MTT reviews custom packaging from 1,000 pieces per design.
sections: Measure the filled products

Record the pump bottle’s maximum width and height with the pump locked and cap fitted. For the pouch, measure in the position it will occupy when filled and sealed, including the spout, seal edges and any bulge. Ask the container suppliers for relevant dimensional ranges; one loose sample does not establish production variation.

Agree who provides filled samples and whether a non-product substitute is permitted. Keep the substitute clearly identified and compare its mass and shape with the real item.
Position the spout away from pressure

Lay each component into a representative insert. A pouch resting against a pump head or a box edge can create a concentrated contact point. Provide a support surface under the pouch body and reserve space around its closure; verify the actual arrangement with the pouch supplier.

Do not place a firm card or insert edge where the closed lid presses on the spout. Compare the loaded set before and after closing the lid. The image is a design concept, not evidence of leak resistance or an approved insert.

Illustrative review: a full refill pouch has a wider bottom than the empty pouch in the artwork file. If the pocket was approved only with the empty pouch, the filled pouch may stand proud and contact the lid. Re-measure the filled item and revise the insert drawing before approving production; this is an example, not an MTT project.
Make removal a separate check

Can a customer lift the bottle by its body without operating the pump? Can the pouch be lifted without pulling its spout? Trial a finger recess, ribbon or a different support height as appropriate. Confirm that any accessory is quoted and supplied separately rather than assumed to be included.

Where the card or insert is removable, observe the order in which the recipient encounters each component. A deep cavity can retain a product but make it hard to remove; a wide opening improves access but may need another retention feature. Compare alternatives using the same representative items and record which condition the brand accepts.
Agree the outer packing route

A presentation insert locates the items; it does not by itself prove protection in a parcel network. Define the complete product and shipping configuration before deciding whether laboratory assessment is needed. ISTA distinguishes screening procedures from distribution simulations; choose a plan with the laboratory for the real route.[1]

Compare the pump-and-refill book box concept with the jar-and-serum insert guide; their different products require different fit checks.
Send a useful quotation brief

Provide filled product dimensions and weights, photos of closures and labels, artwork, card size, quantity by design, destination and who packs the kit. MTT can review the project from 1,000 boxes per design. Confirm actual materials, colours, logo and final fit on a physical sample.
Sources
1. ISTA: test procedure families, accessed 17 November 2026.

imageAlt: Illustrative four-vial fragrance drawer with information card pocket
title: Four-Vial Perfume Drawer Box: Size the Card Pocket and Tray
seoTitle: Four-Vial Perfume Drawer Box: Size the Card Pocket and Tray | MTT
summary: Plan vial channels, card thickness and drawer travel together before approving a fragrance discovery set.
intro: A drawer may hold four sample vials neatly and still jam once cards are added. Measure the finished capped vials and the entire card stack, then check their positions against the sleeve, tray walls and pull. Review the packed sample before approving artwork.
cta: Send the actual product dimensions, quantity per design, destination and project details. MTT reviews custom packaging from 1,000 pieces per design.
sections: Orient the actual vials

Measure every filled vial with its sprayer and cap fitted. Record maximum diameter or width, overall length, label position and any surface that should not rub. If fragrances use different vial suppliers, compare their specified dimensional ranges. Do not size a channel from nominal liquid volume.

Record the order of the four scents and the direction of each label on the insert drawing. Where caps, spray heads or label seams differ between variants, the packing team should use the most relevant representative combinations rather than assuming all four positions behave identically.
Reserve room for the card stack

Measure the full card stack rather than one sheet: include folds, sleeves and any separator. A pocket with a thumb recess lets the recipient remove cards without levering against a vial. If the cards project above the tray or catch inside the sleeve, change the pocket depth or placement and retest with the final stack.
Check drawer movement and removal

Try the empty drawer first, then the insert, vials and cards in sequence. Observe when resistance appears. Check that the ribbon pull is fixed to the tray without obstructing travel, and that users can lift each vial by a suitable surface rather than the sprayer. Compare with the general drawer clearance guide.

Illustrative review: a pocket fits five flat cards but jams with a folded instruction leaflet. Try the approved stack, then look for contact marks on both pocket and sleeve. If a pocket must be deepened, confirm that the change does not reduce the support below the nearby vial channels. This is an engineering example, not a reported customer outcome.
Keep names matched during pack-out

Agree a position map linking each scent, vial label and card version. If the same outer sleeve is used for different assortments, define a clear version identifier and a check at packing. The scent identification checklist addresses that separate control.
Approve the complete package

Request samples with the proposed wrap, board, insert, actual capped vials and card stack. The four-vial drawer concept is illustrative; material and fit need confirmation. If shipping is planned, agree the complete outer pack and testing needs with the appropriate laboratory. ISTA describes tests as applying to a specific packaged product, not an individual material.[1] MTT reviews orders from 1,000 boxes per design.
Sources
1. ISTA: testing a packaged product versus an individual material, accessed 17 November 2026.

imageAlt: Illustrative round perfume gift box; barcode placement needs review on the actual printed tube
title: Barcode on a Round Gift Tube: Review Curvature Before Print
seoTitle: Barcode on a Round Gift Tube: Review Curvature Before Print | MTT
summary: Choose a barcode position and verify the finished curved pack for the intended scanner and retailer.
intro: A barcode that looks clear on a flat artwork proof may wrap around a narrow tube after assembly. Before approving the printed sample, confirm the symbol type, required size, orientation and quiet zones with the barcode provider and retailer. Check the finished tube using the agreed verification method.
cta: Send the actual product dimensions, quantity per design, destination and project details. MTT reviews custom packaging from 1,000 pieces per design.
sections: Start with the use case

Record the intended symbol, data, scanning environment and retailer requirements. A consumer-engagement QR code and a point-of-sale symbol can have different specifications. Ask the relevant barcode authority or retailer for the current application requirements rather than choosing a size from a photo.
Check curvature on the finished tube

GS1 explains that curvature can hide parts of a symbol from a scanner and describes orientation considerations for curved packaging.[1] The result depends on the tube diameter, symbol dimensions and scanning arrangement. Show the printer the actual finished tube and intended orientation before finalising the dieline.

Do not assume a flat proof or a successful scan on one phone establishes compliance with a retailer specification.
Reserve a clear area

Keep the quiet zone free from text, graphics, seams, foil and cuts according to the applicable symbol specification. On a tube, consider the lid overlap and the position of any wrap joint. Agree whether a label or direct print will be used and ensure the printer can maintain placement across the assembled pack.

Illustrative review: a paper wrap is designed flat and its barcode sits near the wrap seam. When assembled, the seam or lid overlap enters the reserved area. Move the symbol in the artwork and review a representative finished pack before releasing the final plate. Confirm all dimensions against the applicable symbol requirements; this example does not set a placement tolerance.
Check the actual surface

Contrast, finish, curvature and glare can affect reading. GS1 identifies contrast and reflections as practical considerations for 2D symbols.[2] Review the final substrate, ink and finish, and obtain verification to the specification required for the application where applicable.

Keep a record of the verified artwork revision, actual tube, substrate, finish and label position. If one of those changes, ask the printer or verification provider whether a new check is appropriate. Reading a code with a camera is a functional check; formal verification uses a calibrated process and the required quality criteria.
Prepare the artwork brief

Send the tube diameter and height, dieline, barcode data and symbol requirements, retailer or scanning context, print finish and quantity per design. A general gift-box barcode checklist covers flat panels; this review focuses on curvature. MTT can discuss packaging projects from 1,000 pieces per design.
Sources

1. GS1 General Specifications: curved surfaces, accessed 17 November 2026.
  2. GS1: 2D barcodes at retail point of sale, accessed 17 November 2026.

imageAlt: Illustrative fragrance box; test specimens must match the project configuration
title: Gift Box Testing: Screening or Distribution Simulation?
seoTitle: Gift Box Screening vs Distribution Simulation | MTT
summary: Compare an early integrity screen and a distribution simulation before selecting a test plan.
intro: A supplier may offer a drop test while a retailer asks for a test reflecting a distribution route. Those are different decisions. Define the packed product and route first, then ask a qualified laboratory which current procedure and acceptance criteria suit the project. A test result applies to the sample and conditions evaluated.
cta: Send the actual product dimensions, quantity per design, destination and project details. MTT reviews custom packaging from 1,000 pieces per design.
sections: Start with the decision

For a new rigid gift box, an early integrity screen can help identify a design weakness before investing in a more representative distribution evaluation. For an established parcel route, the brand may instead need to understand how the complete packed product responds to the forces and sequence associated with that route. Ask the recipient or retailer whether a particular test or report is required.
Understand the distinction

ISTA describes its 1-series procedures as non-simulation integrity tests and its 3-series projects as general simulations. Its 2-series are partial simulations that help refine designs but are not intended to predict shipping performance.[1] Procedure names describe a framework, not a guarantee of damage-free arrival.

As an example, ISTA 1A covers certain individually packaged products up to 68 kg, subject to stated exceptions.[2] Do not select it solely because a gift box weighs less than that limit; the intended distribution and recipient requirements matter.
Define the specimen and criteria

Include the product, closure, insert, presentation box, cushioning and outer shipping carton. Record the packed mass, orientation and each component revision. Agree acceptable product damage and packaging changes before testing; the brand must define product function and cosmetic tolerances with the laboratory.

Use representative filled items or agree a documented substitute. A different bottle, insert or carton can affect the conclusions. See the complete test-brief guide for specimen and acceptance details.

Illustrative review: a wholesale carton is broken down and individual gift boxes continue by courier. A test limited to the first shipment may not address the later parcel route. Explain both stages to the laboratory so it can advise on a suitable plan. This scenario is illustrative and is not a claim of a completed MTT test.
Ask the laboratory to explain the choice

Describe whether individual units travel by parcel, multiple sets travel within a master carton, or pallets are broken down before the final delivery. Ask which test sequence and conditions represent that route, what sample quantity is required, how the specimen is conditioned and what the report will state. Obtain cost, timing and any required retailer format directly from the lab.

Ask whether the specimen represents production materials or a prototype, whether the test is a screen or simulation, and which damage observations are included. A supplier’s offer that only says “drop tested” leaves the specimen, procedure, repetitions and pass criteria unclear. Request the report and reconcile it with the product and carton revision under consideration.
Keep the result with the approved configuration

Retain the report with component drawings, the packing sequence and photographs. If a refill pouch, bottle cap, insert or shipping carton changes, compare it to the tested configuration and consult the lab or product owner about additional work. MTT can review packaging briefs from 1,000 pieces per design; lab testing and its fees are agreed separately.
Sources

1. ISTA: test procedure families, accessed 17 November 2026.
  2. ISTA: Procedure 1A overview, accessed 17 November 2026.
